features.headline: Patriots need to fix defensive effort — especially if Drake Maye misses time
features.desc: New England has given up 80 points over the past two games. The bye week will allow the team to reset.
body: MUNICH — If quarterback Drake Maye misses time with the ankle injury he suffered on Sunday, the New England Patriots will likely need to rely more on defense to salvage the post-Week-11-bye part of their schedule.

That's not a comforting thought after what's unfolded the last two weeks, with Sunday's 35-10 bludgeoning by the Detroit Lions in Munich coming after the defense was sliced up by the Green Bay Packers in a 45-27 defeat the week prior.

Yes, the Lions and Packers are two of the NFL's upper-echelon teams, playing in perhaps the best division, the NFC North. But that's no excuse for what the defense has produced in its last eight quarters.
The unit hasn't met the most basic standard of what coach Mike Vrabel preaches as the No. 1 part of team identity.
They aren't winning the "effort and finish" game.
Veteran safety Kevin Byard, one of six team captains, didn't sugarcoat it when dissecting how the Lions took it to them.
"They played harder than us. They played more physical than us," he said. "And as a defense, that feels like a slap in the face that we let them play harder."
Byard noted Lions receivers blocking way down the field on screen plays, and offensive linemen pushing the pile into the end zone for a touchdown.
The Patriots provided little resistance — allowing a season-high 4.5 yards before contact per rush (not including kneel-downs), per ESPN Research. The previous high was 2.85 yard per rush.
The Lions became the first team with 300 passing yards and 150 rushing yards in a game against the Patriots since the Chiefs in Week 1 of the 2017 season.

features.headline: What's working — and not working — for LeBron James, Philadelphia 76ers
features.desc: We talked to several coaches, executives and scouts about the 11-3 Sixers in an attempt to get a consensus opinion on their start.
body: There are few people on the planet more qualified to speak about what it's like to be a part of a nascent LeBron James-led group with immediate super-team expectations than former NBA sharpshooter Mike Miller.

As a member of the Miami Heat for the first three years of the Heatles' run (2010-13) who again teamed up with James for the tumultuous first season of the superstar's second stint with the Cleveland Cavaliers (2014-15), Miller knows life in the LeBron pressure cooker.

"Everywhere he went, you would find out real quickly who's going to be able to step out there and who's not," said Miller, who now is an agent representing NBA players as the president of LIFT Sports Management. "It's different.
Every shot now, crowd-wise, everything becomes magnified. I've had some good success personally [before playing with James], but nothing on the level of where you really test yourself on that stage.
"That's the reason I chose Miami. I wanted to know if I was going to s—- myself, or perform?"
So far, for the most part, the Philadelphia 76ers have performed fantastically.

The Sixers won eight of their first nine games, including an opening-night victory at Madison Square Garden to spoil the New York Knicks' ring night. They came back from down 29 points to beat the Cavaliers.
And they went on the road to avenge a previous loss to the Detroit Pistons, last season's No. 1 seed in the Eastern Conference.

But two blowout losses in their last four games in Cleveland — when James and Joel Embiid combined to shoot 3-for-21 and had eight turnovers — and at home against their longtime rivals in the Boston Celtics — which caused Jaylen Brown to admit afterward how frustrated he was by his showing — brought them back down to earth.

features.headline: Which NBA players have the most triple-doubles of all time?
features.desc: Russell Westbrook holds the NBA record for most triple-doubles in a career. See who else joins him on the list.
body: Russell Westbrook has more than earned the nickname Mr. Triple Double.
In basketball, a triple-double is when a player compiles a double-digit total in three of five statistical categories (assists, blocks, points, rebounds and steals) over the course of a game.
Blocks and steals were officially recorded by the NBA starting in the 1973-74 season. No player in NBA history has recorded more triple-doubles than Westbrook.
On May 10, 2021, Westbrook became the NBA's career leader in triple-doubles, tallying 28 points, 13 rebounds and 21 assists for the Washington Wizards in a 125-124 loss against the Atlanta Hawks.
It marked the 182nd triple-double of Westbrook's career, passing Oscar Robertson for the most on the all-time list.
Nikola Jokić also has since passed Robertson, whose record stood for more than 47 years.
Westbrook had already broken Robertson's record for the most triple-doubles in a single NBA season (41), recording 42 during the 2016-17 campaign.

features.headline: Who has scored the most goals in NHL history?
features.desc: Alex Ovechkin holds the record for the most individual career goals in NHL history. Which other players are at the top of the list?
body: At the time of his retirement in 1999, Wayne Gretzky owned or shared 61 NHL records, including the mark for the most career goals. "The Great One" finished his illustrious 20-year career with an NHL-record 894 goals in 1,487 games. It is a mark that stood until Alex Ovechkin broke it in April 2025.

With Gretzky in attendance, Ovechkin scored his 895th career goal in a 4-1 loss to the New York Islanders. Ovechkin's record-breaking goal came in the 1,487th game of his NHL career, the same as Gretzky's career total.
The 2026-27 NHL season marks the 22nd for Ovechkin, who looks to add to his career goals total and put even more separation between him and the rest of the field.

features.headline: 2026-27 MLB free agency, trade grades: Offseason analysis
features.desc: We've got you covered with grades and analysis on every winter signing and big offseason trade.
body: The 2026-27 MLB offseason is officially here, and we have you covered with grades and analysis for every major signing and trade as this winter — which is expected to include a labor stoppage — unfolds.
Whether it's a franchise-changing free agent signing or an unexpected blockbuster trade, we'll weigh in with what it all means for next season and beyond.

ESPN MLB experts Bradford Doolittle and David Schoenfield will evaluate each move as it happens, so follow along here — this story will continue to be updated. Check back in for all the most recent analysis.

The Red Sox weren't high on anybody's list of teams likely to sign Jake Bauers given they already have an All-Star first baseman in Willson Contreras, but this signing is an early candidate for best move of the offseason.

The grade reflects two thoughts: (1) that Bauers' breakout — he finished 11th in the majors in OPS and third in on-base percentage this past season — is for real; and (2) that the contract is a steal at $14.5 million per year.

Bauers will be entering his age-31 season, and, of course, spent years struggling in the majors before finally figuring things out, so while there would generally be concern that his 2026 season was a fluke, all the advanced metrics suggest the opposite.
His Statcast numbers: 93rd percentile bat speed, 94th percentile hard-hit rate, 93rd percentile chase rate, 98th percentile walk rate.
Those are real skills that aren't going to diminish overnight and should allow him to remain a productive hitter (he even hit left-handers well, so should project as a full-time player).
